name: Posture / frame / body language

lead: Posture, frame and body language practices use an upright, open and expansive stance so you look taller, broader and more confident while standing and moving. The visual change is immediate.

The chain: open posture gives a taller, broader impression, which makes you look and feel more confident. Studies show small effects on how powerful people feel; the hormonal and behavioural effects reported for power posing in 2010 have not replicated well, and reviews find a reliable effect on feelings of power but not physiology.

paras: People practise standing tall with shoulders back, an open chest and head level, and use power poses before events. It is combined with back and core training and is a free habit that can show in photos right away.
No direct risks reported. There is ongoing disagreement about effect sizes for the feeling-of-power research.

angle.text: Users hold an upright, open stance, sometimes as power posing, so they look taller, broader and more confident while standing. The visual change is immediate; hormone and behaviour claims from posing have replicated poorly, while effects on how people feel are better supported.

lead: In looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities, "posture", "frame" and "body language" refer to how a person holds and moves the body, with the belief that upright, open and expansive postures make a person look and feel more confident and attractive. "Power posing" is a closely related and widely publicised version.

Research on posture reports that confident postures can influence self-evaluation and mood, but the hormonal and behavioral claims of power posing have not replicated well.[1][2] Reviews find a reliable effect on feelings of power but not on physiology.[1]

paras: Briñol, Petty and Wagner (2009) found that people writing self-descriptions in a confident posture rated themselves more favorably than those in a doubtful posture, and Riskind and Gotay (1982) reported more stress in hunched postures.[2] Open posture was rated as more capable in counseling settings (Ridley and Asbury, 1988).[2] Peper et al. (2018) reported better math scores with erect posture.[2]

Carney, Cuddy and Yap (2010) reported that expansive poses raised testosterone and lowered cortisol in 42 participants. Ranehill et al. (2015) replicated only the felt-power effect, and in 2016 Carney said she no longer believed the effects were real.[1] A 2022 review of 128 studies by Körner et al. found reliable effects on thoughts and feelings, none on physiology and unclear effects on behavior; Cuddy and colleagues' 2018 meta-analysis reported evidential value for postural feedback.[1]
Forum members discuss "frame" as an overall presence combining posture, movement and confidence. These are community beliefs; no published trial tests them as appearance methods.
Studies of posture and mood exist, and power-posing trials are summarized above, but no studies were found on "frame" as defined by looksmaxxing communities.[1][2]

timeline.event: Carney, Cuddy and Yap publish the power pose study.[1]
Körner et al. review of 128 studies.[1]
